blocks.cap: Registry sub-level, the room where absence is kept

blocks.p: Somewhere in the dark ahead, a printer breathed out a page.

The registry floor was two levels below the dying plant and the kind man, past a door that read his borrowed card and decided, after a pause long enough to make his scalp prickle, that he was allowed.

Inside, the cold was no longer a thread. It was the weather of the room. Rows of grey cabinets stood in the half-light like a congregation that had been waiting a long time, and the only sound was the printer he had heard through the floor. It was a single machine at the end of the central aisle, breathing out a page every few minutes into a tray already thick with its own patience.

He walked toward it past drawers labelled in a hand too even to be a hand. He understood as he walked that this was not a place where records were stored. It was a place where records were kept alive. Fed, certified, renewed, so that the people they described could be quietly held in whatever condition the building preferred them in.
The page in the tray was his brother.

doc.title: Civil Veil Division. Registry. Status Verification

blocks.p: The page beneath it was the same. And the one below that, the same, the same. A stack of identical certifications climbed back through the days like sediment, each one a small official act of looking at an empty chair and writing present.

He lifted the stack, and the dates ran backward under his thumb. Three days. A week. Two. Then the pattern broke. The oldest pages in the tray were different. They were not automatic. They had been signed, once, by a hand, before the machine took over. And the hand that started the lie had written a single initialled note in the margin of the first one, a note no automatic system would ever produce, in ink gone the brown of old blood.
Per consultation. Y. He asked so little.

Rei stood in the cold congregation with the proof in his hands, and he felt the shape of it close around him the way the cold closed around a stranger at Gin's threshold. Someone had begun this by hand. Someone had sat at a desk in late July and made the first false certification himself, willingly, gratefully, because a consultation had asked so little of him and given him, Rei could only assume, something he wanted very much. Then he had taught the machine to do the rest. He had set the absence to renew itself at six every morning and walked away into a personal leave for his health. And the form had been filing itself ever since. A wound that had learned to bleed on schedule, keeping Rei's brother present in the only ledger that could ever have declared him gone.

He should have left. He photographed the signed pages and he should have turned for the door. Instead the cold pulled him sideways, down a row he had no reason to enter, the way grief pulls a hand toward a drawer it should not open.

The cabinets here were older. Their labels were names, and the names had small coloured tabs, and after the third one he understood the colours. Green was active. Green was the lie. There were more green tabs in this row than a building should ever need. A whole quiet harvest of people the registry was certifying present, each with a tray, each with a printer somewhere breathing them alive at six in the morning. Beside each of the oldest, in the same brown ink, was the same initialled note. Per consultation. Y.

The Healer had been busy. The Healer had been busy for much longer than Gin's three days, asking so little of so many, and filing each favour in a room two floors below the kindest man Rei had ever met.

He thought of the classified page in Gin's book, the one with the heaviest stamp. Component One. Catalogue. Identification and detailed profiling of all practitioners at Level 3 and above. He had read it at the kitchen table as a word on paper. Now he was standing inside it. This was what cataloguing looked like when someone had their hand on the drawer. A name, a tab, a status, a printer. The building did not need to find a person to hold him. It only needed to keep writing down that he was where it wanted him to be.

At the end of the row the labels reached the U's. He found the drawer before he had decided to look for it. UEDERA. Inside there was one folder with a green tab and his brother's name on it, thick with six years of assessments, every one of them reading C.

There was no second folder. Rei went through the drawer twice with cold fingers, and then the drawers on either side of it in case a card had been misfiled. There was nothing with his name on it anywhere. He remembered a line from the preface to Gin's Chapter Four, written on a Wednesday when they had eaten ramen and Rei had fallen asleep on the couch. Rei's file in the CVD system does not exist. He has never been formally assessed. He had read it as a fact. Standing in this room, he read it again as a piece of work. Somebody had kept that drawer empty for nineteen years, in a building whose whole purpose was to fill it.
He closed the drawer very gently, as though the empty space inside it could be bruised.

One drawer was already open. Rei had not opened it. It hung an inch out into the aisle as if it had just been consulted. The file inside was not green, and it was not under any name he knew. It was a register of the registry, an index, and the entry it lay open at was not a person. It was a seat.

The same language. The same machine-even hand. But it was applied not to a man but to a chair in some other ledger entirely, a seat among the Thirteen, which the building was keeping open the way it kept his brother active. By writing the desired condition down every morning until reality was too embarrassed to disagree.

Rei looked at the word null-emotive and thought of the Kuroda compound, and of the fold, and of the word that had settled in him there with no pity in it. Duty. The building had a name for this seat, and it was the wrong one. Nobody here had looked closely enough to see what kind of chair it was. He understood, looking at it, that he had wandered out of his brother's disappearance and into the edge of something that used the same pen. Whatever was thinning the wall was also a clerk. It did its largest work on the smallest paper.

The cold sharpened, the way a held breath sharpens just before it is let go. He became aware that the open drawer had not been left open for the room. It had been left open for him. The borrowed credential that should not exist had been an error that walked him down two floors and along one row to a drawer that hung into the aisle at exactly the height of his eye. And somewhere a kind, busy thing was watching what he did with a vacancy it had gone to the trouble of showing him.

He did the only thing he knew how to do. He breathed out and let his attention go loose, and he looked at the drawer the way a bored intern looks at a drawer. It did not help. Whatever was watching had not come to measure his rank. It had come to see what he wanted.

The favour had found him. It had not asked anything yet. For now it was only letting him read, letting him feel the seam between a brother kept present and a seat kept empty, and trusting, the way it trusted everyone, that once he saw how little it asked, he would want very much to be helped.

He came up out of the building into the full weight of the August morning, and the city did not know. That was the thing that nearly took his legs out on the steps of the Directorate. Tokyo was going about Obon. The lantern strings were up between the lampposts for the dead who were allowed to come home. A woman was arranging chrysanthemums in a bucket outside a convenience store, and a child was being walked to the pool with a towel around his neck. And two floors below all of it a machine was certifying Rei's brother alive on a schedule, and none of these warm, ordinary, breathing people would ever take a ticket in that line.
He had the photographs in his phone and a borrowed wound on a lanyard he had not given back, and he stood in the heat, shivering. He was a stranger to the cold now, wherever he carried it.

The cicadas ground on. Somewhere a temple bell did its slow work over the rooftops, the sound that is supposed to carry to the other side, and Rei thought about which side his brother was on. Not dead. The registry insisted he was not dead. Only active. Only present. Only renewed at six each morning by a form that had learned to file itself the moment a tired official decided a favour had asked so little of him.

He thought about Sekine's dying plant and the chair with no one in it. He thought about a row of green tabs and a drawer that had opened itself to a vacant seat. And he understood that the briefing they had kept quiet was the truest document in the building. Not a thing said, but a thing carefully not said, an absence administered so smoothly that the only way to read it was to become the kind of person who reads absences. Over three days in his brother's cold home, he had become that person.

He took out the lanyard one more time, there on the steps, in the lantern light and the heat, and looked at the authority of a man who was not gone. He could give it back. He could walk into the ordinary morning and let the form file itself for ever.

He put it back in his pocket, next to Gin's useless key. He would come back tomorrow, before six, and be standing at the printer when it tried to renew his brother. He would see for himself whether an absence administered could be an absence revoked. Or whether the only thing his borrowed key really opened was the next room in a trap that had been certifying him, too, as present and accounted for, from the moment he took a ticket.
